column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: The study of fungi is called ___.
column28: Mycology is the study of fungi (myco- means fungus, -ology means the study of). A scientist who studies fungi is a mycologist.
column29: It starts with the same prefix as mycelium and ends with the word part that means "the study of."

column9: Fungi are **heterotrophs**. What does that mean?
column14: They depend on other organisms for food
column15: They make their own food from sunlight, like plants do
column16: They make food from chemicals in rocks
column17: They get all their energy from water
column28: A heterotroph depends on other organisms for food. Fungi can't make their own food because they lack chlorophyll and are not photosynthetic. Making food from sunlight is what autotrophs like plants do.
column29: Fungi have no chlorophyll. So where must their food come from?

column9: Fungal cell walls are made of ___, while plant cell walls are made of cellulose.
column28: Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, the same tough material in insect and crab shells. Plant cell walls are made of cellulose. This is one of the reasons fungi are not plants.
column29: It's the same tough material found in the shells of insects and crabs.

column9: What are **hyphae**?
column14: Tiny reproductive cells that are carried by the wind
column15: Thin, thread-like structures that form the body of a fungus
column16: Sacs that hold a fungus's spores until they are released
column17: The green, food-making cells found inside a lichen
column28: Hyphae (one is a hypha) are thin, thread-like structures that form the "body" of a fungus. They grow and branch until they cover and digest the food source. Tiny reproductive cells are spores, and the green cells in a lichen are algae or cyanobacteria.
column29: Picture the fuzz on a moldy slice of bread. What is that fuzz made of?

column9: What is a **mycelium**?
column14: A single spore
column15: The cap of a mushroom
column16: A mass of hyphae
column17: A sac that holds spores
column28: A mycelium is a mass of hyphae. It is the living body of the fungus and is usually hidden in soil, wood, or another food source. A mycelium may fill a single ant or cover many acres.
column29: It is the living body of the fungus, usually hidden underground or inside its food.

column9: Most fungi reproduce by releasing spores into the air or water.
column28: True. Most fungi reproduce with microscopic spores. A mushroom or puffball can release clouds containing millions of spores, and wind, water, or animals carry them to new places.
column29: Think of a puffball releasing a cloud of dust when you step on it.

column9: Most fungi are multicellular. Which fungus is unicellular (one-celled)?
column14: Mushroom
column15: Bread mold
column16: Puffball
column17: Yeast
column28: Yeast is a one-celled fungus. Mushrooms, bread mold, and puffballs are multicellular fungi made of many hyphae.
column29: Three of these are big enough to see because they are built from many hyphae. Which one can you see only under a microscope?

column9: *Rhizopus*, black bread mold, belongs to which phylum of fungi?
column14: Ascomycota
column15: Basidiomycota
column16: Zygomycota
column17: Imperfect fungi
column28: Black bread mold is in Zygomycota, the common molds. Ascomycota are the sac fungi, Basidiomycota are the club fungi, and the imperfect fungi can only reproduce asexually.
column29: Think about where bread mold makes its spores: in round cases on the tips of upright hyphae. Which phylum does that?

column9: The mushrooms usually found on pizza are sac fungi (Ascomycota).
column28: False. Mushrooms, shelf fungi, and puffballs are club fungi (Basidiomycota), which make spores on the ends of club-shaped structures. Sac fungi make spores in sacs.
column29: Each group's name describes the shape of its spore-making structure. Picture what is on the gills under a mushroom cap.

column9: What does it mean when fungi are **saprophytes**?
column14: They make their own food from sunlight
column15: They live inside a living host and harm it
column16: They live in a partnership where both benefit
column17: They feed on dead or decaying organisms
column28: A saprophyte feeds on dead or decaying organisms. A fungus that lives inside a living host and harms it is a parasite, and fungi in partnerships where both benefit, like lichens, are mutualists. Fungi never make their own food from sunlight.
column29: Where do you usually find mushrooms growing: on a healthy tree, or on a rotting log?

column9: Which of these is a fungus?
column14: Moss
column15: Mushroom
column16: Kelp
column17: Fern
column28: A mushroom is the fruiting body of a fungus. Moss and ferns are plants, and kelp is a brown alga (a protist). All three of those have chlorophyll and make their own food.
column29: Three of these choices can make their own food with chlorophyll.

column9: Match each group of fungi to its key reproduction fact.
column14: Zygomycota :: Make spores in sporangia on the tips of hyphae
column15: Ascomycota :: Make spores inside tiny sacs
column16: Basidiomycota :: Make spores on the ends of club-shaped structures
column17: Imperfect fungi :: Can only reproduce asexually
column28: Fungi are classified by how they reproduce. Zygomycota (common molds) make spores in sporangia, Ascomycota (sac fungi) make spores in sacs, Basidiomycota (club fungi) make spores on club-shaped ends, and imperfect fungi only reproduce asexually.
column29: Recall one example of each group, then think about where that example makes its spores.

column9: Fungi can grow into new individuals from broken pieces of hyphae.
column28: True. Wind and water can carry pieces of hyphae to new places. If there is enough moisture and food, a piece can grow into a new fungus.
column29: Hyphae are the living body of the fungus. Can a broken-off piece keep growing?

column9: A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and what?
column14: Green algae or cyanobacteria
column15: Moss or liverworts
column16: Tree bark or rock
column17: Ferns or horsetails
column28: A lichen is a symbiotic relationship between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner: green algae or cyanobacteria. Lichens often grow on bark or rock, but the bark is just where they live, not a partner.
column29: The partner has to do photosynthesis and be small enough to live among the fungus's hyphae.

column9: Ringworm is a common skin infection that causes a red, ring-shaped rash. What causes it?
column14: A parasitic worm
column15: A fungus
column16: A protist
column17: A virus
column28: Despite its name, ringworm has nothing to do with worms. It is caused by a fungus, like athlete's foot and yeast infections. The "worm" name comes from the ring-shaped rash.
column29: Don't trust the name. Which kingdom loves warm, damp skin?

column9: Fungi are often called nature's recyclers. Why?
column14: They make most of the oxygen that other living things breathe in
column15: They turn sunlight into food that animals can eat
column16: They break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil
column17: They eat living animals and keep their numbers down
column28: As fungi digest dead logs, leaves, and animals, they break them down and return nutrients to the soil for plants to use. Fungi don't photosynthesize, so they don't make oxygen or turn sunlight into food.
column29: Think about what happens to a fallen log in the forest over many years.

column9: Which are ways fungi are different from plants? Select all that apply.
column14: Fungi have roots that absorb water
column15: Fungi lack chlorophyll
column16: Fungi can't make their own food by photosynthesis
column17: Fungi have cells with a nucleus
column28: Fungi lack chlorophyll, are not photosynthetic (so they can't make their own food), and never reproduce by seeds. Both fungi and plants are eukaryotic (their cells have nuclei), most fungi are multicellular, and fungi have hyphae, not roots.
column29: Think about how a plant makes its food and how it makes new plants.

column9: Noah forgets a carton of strawberries on the counter. A week later, one berry is covered in white fuzz topped with tiny round black heads on thin stalks. What are the black heads?
column14: Tiny mushrooms
column15: Colonies of bacteria
column16: Seeds from the strawberry
column17: Sporangia, which make spores
column28: The fuzz is hyphae, and the round heads on the tips of the upright hyphae are sporangia, the structures that make spores. When they break open, spores spread to new food. Mushrooms belong to club fungi, bacteria don't grow upright stalks, and the strawberry's own seeds sit on its skin, not on top of the fuzz.
column29: The mold has to release something so it can spread to new fruit.

column9: Morels, truffles, and yeast all belong to which group of fungi?
column14: Sac fungi (Ascomycota)
column15: Club fungi (Basidiomycota)
column16: Common molds (Zygomycota)
column17: Imperfect fungi
column28: Morels, truffles, yeast, and the fungus in most lichens are sac fungi (Ascomycota), which make their spores in sacs. Mushrooms are club fungi, bread mold is a common mold, and Penicillium is an imperfect fungus.
column29: Morels look a bit like mushrooms, but they are not in the mushroom group.

column9: Most fungi that cause diseases in humans are imperfect fungi.
column28: True. The imperfect fungi, which can only reproduce asexually, cause most fungal diseases in humans, such as yeast infections, athlete's foot, and ringworm.
column29: Think about the group that is "missing" the sexual part of reproduction.

column9: How does a fungus get food from the log it is growing on?
column14: It surrounds small pieces of wood and swallows them whole
column15: It makes sugar from sunlight using chlorophyll in its cap
column16: It pulls food up from the soil through its long roots
column17: Its hyphae digest the wood with enzymes and absorb it
column28: Fungi digest their food outside their bodies. The hyphae grow into the food, give off enzymes that break it down, and absorb the nutrients. Fungi don't swallow food like animals, can't photosynthesize, and have no roots.
column29: Fungi have no mouth and no chlorophyll. How else could a living thing break food down?

column9: Most fungi are parasites that feed on living hosts.
column28: False. Most fungi are saprophytes that feed on dead or decaying material. Only some fungi are parasites.
column29: Think about what happens to most fallen leaves and logs in a forest.

column9: After soccer season, Tyler's feet itch, and the skin between his toes is cracked and peeling. He wore the same damp socks all week. What is the most likely cause?
column14: A virus that spreads through coughs and sneezes
column15: A fungus that grows on the skin and feeds on it
column16: A protist that is carried by mosquitoes
column17: Bacteria from a small cut that got infected
column28: Itchy, cracked, peeling skin between the toes after a week of damp socks is athlete's foot, a fungal infection (caused by an imperfect fungus) that thrives in warm, damp places like sweaty socks and shoes. Viruses spread by coughs cause colds and flu, mosquito-borne protists cause malaria, and an infected cut would be one sore spot, not peeling skin between all the toes.
column29: What kind of organism thrives in warm, damp, dark places like sweaty socks?

column9: A fungus spore can drift for miles. What does it need when it lands in order to grow into a new fungus?
column14: Enough moisture and food
column15: Sunlight for photosynthesis
column16: Soil with seeds in it
column17: Another spore to fuse with right away
column28: If enough moisture and food are present, a spore (or a piece of hyphae) can grow into a new fungus. Fungi don't photosynthesize, so they don't need sunlight, and they don't use seeds.
column29: Think about why bread gets moldy in a damp bag but not in a dry cupboard.

column9: Put the events in the 1928 discovery of penicillin in order.
column14: Penicillin became an antibiotic used to treat infections
column15: A mold accidentally started growing on one of the plates
column16: The mold, Penicillium, was found to make a bacteria-killing substance
column17: Fleming noticed the bacteria were gone in a ring around the mold
column18: Alexander Fleming grew Staphylococcus bacteria on culture plates
column28: Fleming was growing Staphylococcus aureus in 1928 when a mold landed on a plate. He noticed bacterial colonies were absent around the mold. The mold was Penicillium, and its bacteria-killing substance became the antibiotic penicillin.
column29: An observation has to come before an explanation, and an explanation before a medicine.

column9: Many fungi don't grow tall enough to get above the "boundary layer" of still air near the ground. How do they get their spores to new places?
column14: They grow seeds with papery wings that drift away on the breeze
column15: They swim to new places using whip-like flagella
column16: They shoot spores out or let wind, water, or animals carry them
column17: They wait for bees to carry their pollen to new places
column28: Fungi solve the boundary-layer problem in two ways: they shoot their spores, or they use animals, water, or wind for dispersal. Once a spore is caught by something, it can be carried long distances. Fungi don't make seeds or flowers, and the fungi in our four groups don't swim with flagella.
column29: Spores need a ride. What can carry tiny, light things?

column9: Morels can sell for $100–200 per pound. Which fact best explains the high price?
column14: They grow on almost every lawn all summer long
column15: They are hard to farm and mostly appear a few weeks each spring
column16: They make their own food by photosynthesis, so they taste sweet
column17: They are the only kind of fungus that people can eat
column28: Morels are very hard to farm, so most are hunted in the wild during a few weeks each spring. The supply is small, so the price is high. They don't make their own food, and many other fungi are edible.
column29: Think about supply: how easy is it to get morels?

column9: Mushrooms seem to pop up overnight after a rain. What best explains this?
column14: A spore that lands during the rain grows into a full mushroom overnight
column15: Heavy rain washes buried mushrooms up from deep in the soil
column16: Mushrooms use rainwater to make their own food overnight
column17: The hidden mycelium was already there and quickly pushed up mushrooms
column28: The living body of the fungus, the mycelium, has been growing hidden in the soil for a long time. When moisture and temperature are right, it quickly pushes up mushrooms, which are only the fruit of the fungus. A single spore can't become a mushroom overnight.
column29: The mushroom is only the "fruit." Where was the rest of the fungus all along?

column9: Which are ways fungi help humans? Select all that apply.
column14: Fungi make most of the oxygen we breathe
column15: Molds are used to make cheeses like blue cheese
column16: Fungi cause athlete's foot and ringworm
column17: Many mushrooms and morels are eaten as food
column18: Some molds are sources of antibiotics
column19: Yeast is used to make bread rise
column28: Yeast raises bread, Penicillium and other molds give us antibiotics, many mushrooms are food, and molds give blue cheese its veins and flavor. Athlete's foot and ringworm are harms, and fungi can't photosynthesize, so they don't make oxygen.
column29: One wrong choice is a harm, and one describes something fungi can't do.

column9: Dutch elm disease and oak wilt have killed many trees in Wisconsin. What causes these diseases?
column14: Sac fungi that infect the trees
column15: Water molds that rot the roots
column16: Viruses spread by deer
column17: Too little sunlight in crowded forests
column28: Dutch elm disease and oak wilt are caused by sac fungi (Ascomycota), a group that includes many plant pathogens. The fungus clogs the tree's water-carrying tissue, and the tree wilts and dies.
column29: Recall the plant diseases listed in the same group as yeast, morels, and truffles.

column9: Fungi reproduction is classified by the way they form spores and by the ___ of the structure in which the spores are made.
column28: Fungi reproduction is classified by (1) the way they form the spores and (2) the shape (type) of the structure in which spores are made. That's why the groups have names like sac fungi and club fungi.
column29: Think about the names "sac" fungi and "club" fungi. What do those names describe?

column9: Marisol mixes yeast into bread dough and sets it in a warm spot. An hour later, the dough has doubled in size. What made it rise?
column14: The yeast made oxygen gas by doing photosynthesis
column15: The yeast's spores soaked up water from the dough and swelled up
column16: The yeast broke down sugar and released carbon dioxide gas
column17: The yeast's long hyphae grew all through the dough
column28: Yeast is a one-celled fungus. It breaks down sugar (fermentation) and gives off carbon dioxide gas, which forms bubbles that make the dough rise. Yeast has no chlorophyll, so it can't photosynthesize, and as a one-celled fungus it doesn't form hyphae.
column29: Look at the little holes in a slice of bread. What made them?

column9: In a mushroom-forming fungus, the hidden mycelium, not the mushroom you can see, is the part that makes and releases spores.
column28: False. The part you can see (the fruiting body, like a mushroom) is the part that makes and releases spores. The hidden mycelium is the living, feeding body of the fungus.
column29: The visible part is called the "fruit" of the fungus. What is its job?

column9: What is a **germ tube**?
column14: A tube that carries water from the mycelium up a mushroom stalk
column15: The first hypha that grows out of a spore
column16: An opening where spores leave a sac
column17: A hollow stalk that holds sporangia
column28: A germ tube is a growing spore's first (initial) hypha. It grows and branches into more hyphae, which eventually form a mycelium.
column29: "Germ" here means sprouting, like a seed germinating.

column9: Which are ways fungi can be harmful? Select all that apply.
column14: Fungi shade out crops by growing tall leaves
column15: Fungi release seeds that grow into weeds
column16: Molds spoil foods like bread and fruit
column17: Some wild mushrooms are poisonous to eat
column18: Some fungi cause crop diseases that ruin harvests
column28: Some mushrooms are deadly, molds spoil food, and fungi such as Fusarium (which causes head blight) ruin wheat and barley. Fungi have no leaves and never make seeds, so the choices about tall leaves and seeds can't happen.
column29: Two choices describe structures that fungi don't have.

column9: A student finds an organism growing as a network of white threads through a rotting log. Its cells have walls but no chloroplasts, and it reproduces with spores. Which kingdom does it belong to, and why?
column14: Fungi, because it is a heterotroph made of hyphae that reproduces by spores
column15: Plantae, because its cells have cell walls and it makes spores like a fern does
column16: Protista, because every organism that makes spores is a protist
column17: Animalia, because it can't make its own food
column28: Threads (hyphae) feeding on a dead log, spores, and no chloroplasts all point to Kingdom Fungi. Plants have chloroplasts, many organisms besides protists make spores, and animals have no cell walls.
column29: Having no chloroplasts rules out one kingdom right away. Which kingdom grows as a network of threads?

column9: Kayla says mushrooms should be classified as plants because they grow out of the ground and don't move. Which evidence best shows she is wrong?
column14: Mushrooms grow best in shady, damp places
column15: Some kinds of mushrooms are poisonous to people and pets
column16: Mushrooms have no chlorophyll and absorb their food
column17: Mushrooms come in many different colors and sizes
column28: Plants have chlorophyll and make their own food by photosynthesis. Mushrooms lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophs that absorb food, so they are not plants. Growing in shade, being poisonous, and having colors are true of some plants too, so they don't prove anything.
column29: What do plants use to make their food?

column9: Students place a paper disk soaked in mold extract on a plate covered with bacteria. A second disk is soaked in plain water. After 2 days, there is a clear ring 18 mm wide around the mold disk, and bacteria grow right up to the water disk. What is the best conclusion?
column14: Water kills bacteria
column15: Bacteria grow faster near mold
column16: The mold disk blocked the sunlight that the bacteria needed to grow
column17: The mold makes a substance that kills or stops bacteria
column28: The only difference between the disks is the mold extract, and only that disk has a clear ring with no bacteria. So the mold makes a substance that kills or stops bacteria, just like Fleming's Penicillium. The water disk (the control) shows water alone does nothing.
column29: Compare the two disks. What was different, and what happened around only one of them?

column9: After taking antibiotics for two weeks, Jenna gets a yeast infection caused by *Candida*, a fungus that normally lives in small numbers in the body. What is the best explanation?
column14: The antibiotics were made from Candida yeast cells
column15: Antibiotics contain sugars that the yeast cells feed on and multiply
column16: Antibiotics change some of the bacteria into yeast
column17: Antibiotics killed bacteria that keep Candida in check
column28: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not fungi. When the normal, helpful bacteria die off, Candida has less competition and overgrows. This is called an opportunistic infection.
column29: Antibiotics target bacteria. What happens to a fungus when its competitors disappear?

column9: Two groups of pine seedlings grow in sterilized soil. Group A gets soil fungi added to its roots; Group B gets none. After 3 months, Group A is taller and greener, and microscopes show fungal hyphae wrapped around and into Group A's roots. What is the best explanation?
column14: The fungi made sugar by photosynthesis and fed it to the seedlings
column15: The hyphae helped the roots absorb more water and minerals
column16: The fungi added extra chlorophyll to the pine needles
column17: The fungi ate the roots, which made the seedlings grow faster
column28: This root-fungus partnership is called mycorrhizae. The thin hyphae reach far into the soil and pass water and minerals to the roots, and the plant gives the fungus sugar, so both benefit (mutualism). Fungi can't photosynthesize or make chlorophyll.
column29: Hyphae are very thin and can spread far. How could that help a root?

column9: A lichen growing on a sunny rock is moved into a dark cave and kept moist. What will most likely happen to it over time?
column14: The fungus starts making food by photosynthesis to feed its partner
column15: The partner can't make food, so both partners slowly starve
column16: The lichen thrives, because fungi never need light to survive
column17: Only the partner dies; the fungus absorbs food from the bare rock
column28: In a lichen, the green algae or cyanobacteria make food by photosynthesis, which needs light, and pass it to the fungus. In the dark the partner can't make food, and the fungus depends on that food, so both slowly starve. Fungi can't photosynthesize, and bare rock has no food a fungus can absorb. A fungus that feeds on dead material doesn't need light, but the lichen fungus relies on its partner.
column29: Which partner makes the food in a lichen, and what does it need to do that?

column9: Put the steps of how mold takes over a slice of bread in order.
column14: A spore absorbs moisture and sprouts its first hypha
column15: Hyphae branch through the bread, digesting it
column16: Spores floating in the air land on the bread
column17: The spore cases break open and release new spores
column18: Upright hyphae grow with tiny round spore cases on top
column28: A spore lands on food, takes in moisture, and grows a first hypha. Hyphae branch and digest the bread, then upright hyphae form sporangia that release new spores, and the cycle repeats.
column29: The mold has to grow and feed before it can make new spores.

column9: Which of these belong to Kingdom Fungi? Select all that apply.
column14: Slime mold
column15: Morel
column16: Moss
column17: Penicillium
column28: Yeast and morels (sac fungi), puffballs (club fungi), and Penicillium (imperfect fungi) are all fungi. Slime molds are fungus-like protists that have a moving, amoeba-like stage, and moss is a plant with chlorophyll.
column29: One wrong choice is a fungus-like protist, and one is a plant.

column9: Students kept bread slices in four places for 7 days and counted mold spots. All slices were kept in closed, dark containers. Refrigerator (4°C, dry): 0 spots. Counter (22°C, dry): 3 spots. Counter (22°C, damp): 11 spots. Warm cabinet (30°C, damp): 18 spots. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Mold grows most when it is warm and damp
column15: Mold grows most in the cold
column16: Moisture has no effect on mold growth
column17: Mold grows best at room temperature (22°C)
column28: Compare rows that differ in one thing. Dry vs. damp at 22°C: 3 vs. 11 spots, so moisture helps. Damp at 22°C vs. 30°C: 11 vs. 18, and dry at 4°C vs. 22°C: 0 vs. 3, so warmth helps when moisture is the same. The most mold grew where it was both warm and damp, not at room temperature or in the cold.
column29: Compare two rows that differ in only one condition.

column9: A single puffball can release trillions of spores, but only a few ever grow into new puffballs. Why is making so many spores a good strategy?
column14: Spores have to fuse together in large groups before they can grow
column15: Most spores land where they can't grow, so making many helps a few succeed
column16: Each spore can only start growing after all the others die
column17: Extra spores make the puffball heavy enough that the wind can't blow it away
column28: Spores are carried randomly by wind, water, and animals, and most land where there isn't enough moisture or food to grow. Making huge numbers raises the chance that a few land in a good spot.
column29: Think about where most spores end up after the wind carries them.

column9: Match each organism description to its kingdom.
column14: Multicellular; makes food by photosynthesis; cell walls of cellulose :: Plantae
column15: Mostly multicellular; absorbs food from dead material; makes spores; no chlorophyll :: Fungi
column16: One cell with a nucleus; moves with cilia :: Protista
column17: Multicellular; eats its food; no cell walls; moves from place to place :: Animalia
column28: Photosynthesis and cellulose walls mean Plantae. Absorbing food from dead material with no chlorophyll means Fungi. One eukaryotic cell with cilia means Protista. Eating food, moving, and having no cell walls means Animalia.
column29: Find the key clue in each description: photosynthesis, absorbs, cilia, or eats.

column9: The fungus in a lichen gets food from its partner, and the partner gets protection and support. This kind of relationship is called ___.
column28: Both partners benefit, so a lichen is mutualism, a kind of symbiosis. The algae or cyanobacteria make food by photosynthesis, and the fungus provides protection and support.
column29: Recall the ecology word for a partnership where both sides win.

column9: Sam says, "Fungi are more like animals than plants." Which evidence best supports Sam?
column14: Like animals, fungi have cell walls
column15: Like animals, fungi move from place to place
column16: Like animals, fungi can't make their own food
column17: Like animals, fungi grow from seeds
column28: Fungi and animals are both heterotrophs that depend on other organisms for food. Animals have no cell walls, fungi don't move from place to place, and neither one grows from seeds, so those choices aren't true of both.
column29: Check each choice: is it actually true of both fungi and animals?

column9: Which statement correctly compares a mushroom and black bread mold?
column14: The mushroom is a true fungus, but bread mold is a fungus-like protist
column15: Bread mold makes seeds, but mushrooms make spores instead
column16: Mushrooms make their own food, but bread mold has to absorb it
column17: Both are made of hyphae and make spores, but in different structures
column28: Both are fungi made of hyphae that reproduce with spores. Bread mold (common mold) makes spores in sporangia, and mushrooms (club fungi) make spores on club-shaped ends. Fungi never make seeds or their own food.
column29: Both are in the same kingdom. What's different is where the spores are made.

column9: Two hikers find a wild mushroom that looks like a morel. Jake says, "It's spring, and deer already nibbled it, so it's safe to eat." Mia says, "False morels look almost the same and are poisonous, so we shouldn't eat it unless an expert identifies it." Whose reasoning is better, and why?
column14: Mia's, because a poisonous look-alike means its looks can't prove it's safe
column15: Jake's, because a morel-shaped mushroom found in spring must be a morel
column16: Jake's, because a mushroom that deer can eat must be safe for people too
column17: Mia's, because all wild mushrooms are poisonous, even true morels
column28: False morels look a lot like true morels and can be deadly, so appearance alone can't prove the mushroom is safe; only an expert identification can. False morels also come up in spring, and animals can eat mushrooms that poison people, so Jake's evidence doesn't rule out a look-alike. Mia's other reason in choice d is wrong: true morels are edible and prized.
column29: Does either piece of Jake's evidence tell a true morel apart from a false one?
